title: How AI reads your prompt, and how to write one that works

say: How AI reads your prompt, and how to write one that works.
This is the video for module one of Prompt Engineering.
Tools such as ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude and Copilot are built on large language models. Given some text, the model predicts what text should come next. It is not looking up a stored answer.

panel.heading: The model only knows what you give it

say: If your prompt is vague, the most likely reply is vague and average. If it names the reader, the purpose and the format, the reply becomes specific.

say: Models read tokens. A common English word may be one token, but a Yoruba, Hausa or Igbo word may be split into several. As a rough guide, 1,000 tokens is about 750 English words.

panel.heading: Four things to know about the model
items: It reads tokens, chunks of text, not words
The context window limits what it can consider
It can state false facts with confidence
Each new chat starts blank by default

say: The context window is the most it can consider at once, including your prompt, any pasted document and the reply. In a very long chat, earlier details can be dropped. Start a fresh chat and paste a short summary.

say: Confident but false answers are called hallucinations. They happen most with names, exact figures, recent events and references. Check anything you will publish or act on.

say: For example, Halima coordinates a women's cooperative in Kaduna. She needs to tell 40 members the meeting venue has changed. Her first prompt gets a formal, generic letter with blanks where the facts should be.

panel.heading: One task, two prompts
left: Write a message about a venue change

say: Her second prompt names the readers, mostly traders aged 30 to 60, the date, the old and new venue, the time, the reason, the channel, and a limit of 60 words.
The reply is 52 words and ready to send. The model did not get smarter. Halima gave it the facts it needed.

panel.heading: One task, two prompts
left: Write a message about a venue change

say: Ngozi works at an NGO in Enugu. She must turn a 9-page field report into a one-page brief. Her task starts with one strong verb: write a one-page decision brief.
Context: the reader is her director, who has 5 minutes before a funder call.
Input: the report pasted between report tags, so the model does not confuse it with her instructions.
Format: four headings, bullet points, under 300 words.
Constraints: use only numbers in the report. Where there is no figure, write NOT STATED.

Examples: a past brief the director praised. Her vague prompt had invented a figure that was not in the report. The six-part prompt gave 270 words with no invented figures, and she still checked every number.

panel.heading: The six-part prompt
panel.rule: Tell it what to do when information is missing: do not guess.

say: List your tasks for one week, then map each by the value of time saved and the risk if it is wrong. Start with high value, low risk tasks.

cards.d: Internal notes, weekly updates, first drafts. Prompt first, then a light check.
Donor reports, financial summaries. Worth prompting, but check every figure and claim.
Grief, apology, decisions about people, legal, medical or financial judgement.

say: High value but high risk work is still worth prompting, with careful checks.

say: Treat anything you type into a public AI tool as information leaving your control.
Never paste passwords, BVN or NIN numbers, bank details, members' phone numbers or private health information. Replace names with roles before you paste a real document.

panel.heading: Never paste what you would not post
items: No members' phone numbers or health information
Replace names with roles, like Member A

say: Remember. The model predicts likely text, so give it the facts. Use the six parts for anything that matters.
And measure honestly. Funmi, a school administrator in Ibadan, saved about 63 hours a year from three prompts, and her checking time did not shrink. Checking is part of the job.

panel.heading: What to keep from this module
items: The model predicts text; it does not look things up
Missing details lead to generic replies
Use the six parts for any task that matters
Measure time saved, including checking time

say: Send a vague prompt and a detailed one for a real message, and compare them. Rebuild one work prompt with all six parts. Then draw your value and risk map with at least eight tasks.
Now continue with the lessons below.
